summary:
ULTRAVIOLET EARTH – An immersive experience to discover our planet We will develop a traveling ultraviolet exhibition, adaptable to different physical spaces in the world, where art and science come together to bring knowledge of our planet closer to people of all ages. Using fluorescent paints, ultraviolet lighting, satellite images and an interactive data jukebox, we will transform official NASA scientific information into visual and sound experiences. We will explore terrestrial phenomena such as storms, forest fires, climate changes, oceans, solar radiation and volcanic activity. The project seeks to convert complex scientific information into educational, participatory and easy-to-understand experiences, especially for children and young people, without excluding the adult public. Its importance lies in generating new forms of learning and environmental awareness, demonstrating that art and technology can bring science closer to society in an accessible, creative and unforgettable way.

details: ULTRAVIOLET EARTH – Immersive scientific exhibition What does it do and how does it work? ULTRAVIOLET EARTH is a traveling artistic, scientific and educational exhibition that transforms different phenomena on our planet into visual and interactive experiences through fluorescent painting, ultraviolet lighting and digital technology. The proposal consists of creating an immersive room that can be installed and adapted to museums, cultural centers, universities, schools and public spaces anywhere. Inside, visitors will tour different thematic stations dedicated to terrestrial phenomena such as forest fires, storms, oceans, volcanic activity, solar radiation and environmental changes. The scientific content will be fed by official and open NASA sources. NASA Worldview and GIBS will be used especially to obtain satellite images, EONET to consult natural events and NASA POWER to access meteorological, solar and climatic parameters. These data will be interpreted and transformed into visual compositions, animations, maps, sounds and works made with fluorescent materials. The intention is to develop an interactive terrestrial data jukebox: a system where the visitor can select a phenomenon and discover its behavior through an audiovisual and artistic experience. What benefits does it have? The main benefit is bringing science closer to audiences who often find it difficult to understand traditional scientific data. Through art, experimentation and interaction, we seek to generate an educational experience accessible to children, young people and adults. It also promotes scientific literacy, curiosity about satellite observation and greater awareness about the environmental changes affecting our planet. What is the expected impact? We seek to develop a replicable and traveling exhibition format, capable of reaching different communities and educational contexts. Its modular design will allow the dimensions, contents and technical resources to be adapted according to the available space. The expected impact is to create new forms of scientific dissemination, awaken vocations related to art, technology and space sciences, and generate a closer relationship between society and the information we obtain from space. What tools, languages, hardware or software will be used? The project contemplates working with: Scientific data: NASA Worldview, GIBS, EONET and NASA POWER. Information integration: official NASA APIs to recover data and images. Digital visualization: an interactive interface developed using web technologies, with JavaScript and data visualization tools. Audiovisual production: animation and editing software to transform data into visual and sound experiences. Hardware: computer, projector, sound system, ultraviolet LED lighting, fluorescent acrylic paints and physical media for the facilities. Interaction: an interface that allows you to select phenomena, consult information and activate different experiences within the room. These tools constitute the technological architecture planned for the development of the prototype and its subsequent implementation. What makes the project creative? His creativity lies in combining two languages that are normally presented separately: scientific research and artistic expression. Ultraviolet light and fluorescent paint allow us to build a visual universe where terrestrial phenomena acquire a new dimension. Data stops being numbers, graphs or satellite images and becomes experiences that can be observed, heard and physically traversed. The proposal also seeks to ensure that the public is not only a spectator, but also an active participant in the exhibition, being able to choose which phenomena to explore and discover the connections between them. What factors do we consider? We especially consider educational accessibility, fidelity to scientific sources, visitor safety, energy consumption, adaptability of assembly and the possibility of reproducing the experience in different countries. Ultraviolet lighting will be selected taking into account eye and skin safety, and appropriate materials will be used for educational and public spaces. ULTRAVIOLET EARTH seeks to demonstrate that art can become a tool to understand our planet and that data obtained from space can also awaken emotions, questions and new forms of knowledge.
